newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu talks tough ahead of U.S. visit.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu talks tough ahead of U.S. visit.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speaking before talks in Washington on rescuing Middle East peace, signalled "no deal" to any halt in Jewish settlement on occupied land.

"We will continue to build in Jerusalem, also on Har Homa. We will continue to build in settlements -- period," Netanyahu said in a speech on Thursday to members of his right-wing Likud party in Tel Aviv.
Senior Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour called the statement, ahead of a meeting between Netanyahu and U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday, another "stone on the grave" of the peace process.
Palestinians insist peace talks can restart only when Israel stops work on a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on a hill called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

Israel demands the Palestinian Authority crack down on "terrorism" as a condition for negotiating again, charging it gave a green light for the resumption of suicide bombings by Moslem militants after a year-long lull.
Clashes have flared daily in the West Bank since Israel broke ground for 6,500 homes for Jews on the pine-covered Jerusalem hill on the road to Bethlehem two weeks ago.

But it was a headline in Israel's biggest newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth -- "U.S. proposes deal: 'no' to terror attacks, 'no' to settlements" -- that appeared to ring alarm bells in the prime minister's office on Wednesday.
Within hours, the prime minister's spokesman issued a statement saying Netanyahu would insist when he meets Clinton on Israel's "right" to settle Jews in East Jerusalem and the rest of the West Bank.
Netanyahu has been under heavy pressure from religious and ultranationalist members of his ruling coalition to press ahead with settlement on biblical land occupied in the 1967 Middle East war.

Israel regards all of Jerusalem as its "eternal and indivisible" capital. The PLO wants East Jerusalem as capital of a Palestinian state and says the new settlement is another link in a chain of Jewish neighbourhoods ringing the city.
Lashing out at the Palestinian Authority, Netanyahu said the self-rule administration had yet to extinguish the "green light for terror".
Asked about the prime minister's remarks, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat told reporters in Gaza: "We are against terrorism -- definite."
Three Israeli women were killed in a suicide blast in Tel Aviv on March 21 and two Palestinians died in botched suicide bombings in Gaza on Tuesday.

Underscoring tensions, Israeli soldiers shot dead a horse that galloped through a security gate into an Israeli settlement in Gaza late on Thursday. Israel Radio said the troops thought it was hauling an explosives-laden cart. No bomb was found.
In the 15th straight day of West Bank violence, Palestinian students in Bethlehem rained stones on Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint while staging a mock funeral for peace. No injuries were reported.
Backing away from inflaming Moslem militants further, Israel suspended its request that the United States extradite Moussa Abu Marzook, a politburo member of the Islamic group Hamas.

Abu Marzook, a long-time resident of the United States, told Reuters in an interview in the New York prison where he has been held without charge or trial since July 1995 that the Israeli government's announcement had not surprised him.

"My understanding is that everything is done," he said, referring to an apparent agreement he would be deported to Jordan. U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno told reporters the 47-year-old Palestinian would remain in U.S. custody.
